# penalties7 <img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="139" alt="" />

Penalties for regularized and Bayesian regression as S7 objects. A penalty
is $\rho(D\beta; \theta)$, made of a linear map $D$, a scalar function
$\rho$ and hyperparameters $\theta$. The object supplies the value with its
normalizing constant, the derivatives in the coefficients and in the
hyperparameters (in closed form for every penalty that ships), the mixed
block, the points where the penalty is not smooth, the proximal operator
where one exists, and, for the quadratic branches, the rank, the null basis
and the log pseudo-determinant that a marginal criterion uses.

Part of the [statmodels7](https://statmodels7.github.io) toolkit.

## Installation

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("statmodels7/penalties7")
```

## The branches

`quadratic_penalty()` carries a fixed positive semidefinite matrix $P$, an
optional map $D$ and one smoothing parameter $\lambda$. Its value is the
negative log-density of the Gaussian prior on $\beta$ with precision
$\lambda D^\top P D$, which is improper when that matrix is singular, as it
is for the second-difference penalty below. The rank, the null basis and the
log pseudo-determinant are computed from the eigendecomposition of
$D^\top P D$ when the object is built.

```{r}
P <- crossprod(diff(diag(6), differences = 2))   # a second-difference penalty
pen <- quadratic_penalty(P)
c(rank = penalty_rank(pen), nullity = ncol(penalty_null_basis(pen)))
penalty_value(pen, rep(1, 6), list(lambda = 1))
```

The `blocks` argument builds the penalty of $I_m \otimes P$, which is the
penalty of a smooth repeated over the levels of a factor, from the single
block $P$. The eigenvalues of the Kronecker product are those of $P$
repeated $m$ times, so the rank, the log pseudo-determinant and the null
basis follow from the small matrix. The large matrix is stored as a sparse
matrix and is never decomposed.

```{r}
blocked <- quadratic_penalty(P, blocks = 50)
c(rank = penalty_rank(blocked), columns = 6 * 50)
```

`additive_penalty()` is a sum of quadratic penalties with a smoothing
parameter on each, $S(\lambda) = \sum_k \lambda_k P_k$, which is the penalty
of an anisotropic tensor-product smooth. The null space of a sum of positive
semidefinite matrices is the intersection of their null spaces and does not
depend on the smoothing parameters, so the rank is computed once, at
construction, from the sum of the components with each one divided by its
largest absolute entry. A count of the nonzero eigenvalues of $S(\lambda)$
itself would fall as the smoothing parameters spread apart.

```{r}
P1 <- crossprod(diff(diag(6), differences = 2))
P2 <- crossprod(diff(diag(6), differences = 1))
add <- additive_penalty(list(P1, P2))
penalty_rank(add)
```

`distrib_penalty()` builds a penalty from a continuous
[distributions7](https://statmodels7.github.io/distributions7/) family. The
value is the negative log-density of the family at the coordinates of
$D\beta$, taken one coordinate at a time for a univariate family, which
gives a separable penalty, and one block at a time for a multivariate
family. `lasso_penalty()` is a Laplace at zero, `elasticnet_penalty()` the
product of a Laplace and a Gaussian, and `heavy_penalty()` a Student t,
whose degrees of freedom can be estimated because the normalizing constant
is part of the value.

```{r}
lasso <- lasso_penalty(n_coef = 3)

penalty_value(lasso, c(1, -2, 0.5), list(lambda = 2))
penalty_kinks(lasso, list(lambda = 2))   # where the density is not smooth
```

`ridge_penalty()` is the Gaussian at zero written by its precision
$\lambda$, which is the quadratic penalty at the identity matrix. It is
therefore built by `quadratic_penalty()` and not by `distrib_penalty()`, and
its hyperparameter is the `lambda` of the quadratic branch. The separable
Gaussian is the same prior written by its standard deviation
$\sigma = 1/\sqrt{\lambda}$, and the two values agree to rounding error. In
the ridge, the lasso, the elastic net, SCAD and MCP a larger `lambda`
shrinks harder; in `heavy_penalty()` the hyperparameter `sigma` is a scale,
and a larger value shrinks less.

```{r}
ridge <- ridge_penalty(n_coef = 3)
penalty_value(ridge, c(1, -1, 2), list(lambda = 1))

# the same prior on the separable branch, written by sigma = 1 / sqrt(lambda)
twin <- distrib_penalty(
  distributions7::fixed(distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), mu = 0),
  n_coef = 3)
penalty_value(twin, c(1, -1, 2), list(sigma = 1))
```

`structured_penalty()` reads a
[parameters7](https://statmodels7.github.io/parameters7/) matrix parameter as
the precision of a Gaussian prior, so the hyperparameters are the free values
of that structure and every derivative comes from its derivative arrays. A
structure meant as a covariance is passed as `parameters7::inverse_of()` of
the structure, which gives a different prior at the same free values. At a
zero log-Cholesky free vector the precision is the identity matrix, and the
penalty equals the ridge at $\lambda = 1$.

```{r}
st <- structured_penalty(parameters7::log_cholesky(3))
st@params
eta <- as.list(stats::setNames(rep(0, length(st@params)), st@params))

c(structured = penalty_value(st, c(1, -1, 2), eta),
  ridge      = penalty_value(ridge, c(1, -1, 2), list(lambda = 1)))
```

`scad_penalty()` and `mcp_penalty()` are defined by their derivative rather
than by a density. Both have the slope $\lambda$ of the lasso at the origin
and become flat far from it, so a large coefficient is not shrunk at all,
while the lasso shrinks every nonzero coefficient by the same amount. The
second hyperparameter (`a` for SCAD, `gamma` for MCP) sets the point
$a\lambda$ or $\gamma\lambda$ beyond which the penalty is flat. Their value
is bounded, so $\exp(-\rho)$ is not integrable and they carry no normalizing
constant. `is_proper()` returns `TRUE` for the penalties that are proper
priors.

```{r}
scad <- scad_penalty(n_coef = 3)
mcp  <- mcp_penalty(n_coef = 3)

vapply(list(ridge = ridge, lasso = lasso, scad = scad, mcp = mcp),
       is_proper, logical(1))

# the derivative: close to lambda near zero, zero past the threshold
b <- c(0.2, 2, 8)
rbind(lasso = penalty_gradient(lasso, b, list(lambda = 1)),
      scad  = penalty_gradient(scad,  b, list(lambda = 1, a = 3.7)),
      mcp   = penalty_gradient(mcp,   b, list(lambda = 1, gamma = 3)))
```

## The proximal operator

`penalty_prox()` evaluates
$\operatorname{prox}_{t\rho}(v) = \arg\min_\beta \{\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\beta -
v\rVert^2 + t\,\rho(\beta;\theta)\}$, the operator that a proximal gradient
method applies after each gradient step. For the quadratic and structured
branches it is a linear solve, under any map. For the Gaussian, Laplace and
elastic-net priors at zero it has a closed form, and for SCAD and MCP it is the
closed piecewise operator, available while the step keeps the problem
convex (a step below $a - 1$ for SCAD and below $\gamma$ for MCP). For any
other separable parent with a smooth log-density it is the global minimizer
among the roots of the stationary condition, coordinate by coordinate. The
separable operators need the identity map or a diagonal one. `has_prox()`
returns `FALSE` for the additive branch, for a separable penalty under a map
that is not diagonal and for a multivariate parent, which have no operator.

```{r}
v <- c(2, -0.4, 0.9)
penalty_prox(lasso, v, step = 1, theta = list(lambda = 1))   # soft threshold
sign(v) * pmax(abs(v) - 1, 0)                                # by hand
```

## Validation

`check_penalty()` compares the derivatives of a penalty with numerical
references computed by numDeriv: the gradient and the Hessian in the
coefficients, the gradient and every entry of the Hessian in the
hyperparameters, and the mixed block. For a quadratic penalty it also checks
the three-point identity of a quadratic form, the log pseudo-determinant, the
rank and the null basis. It does not test the proximal operator. The function is meant
above all for a penalty written outside the package; the article
[Defining a penalty](https://statmodels7.github.io/penalties7/articles/defining-a-penalty.html)
writes one and validates it, and the examples of `check_penalty()` show the
row that fails when a gradient is wrong.

```{r}
res <- check_penalty(ridge_penalty(n_coef = 3), verbose = FALSE)
all(res$status == "OK")
```
